title: A lawyer’s lonely fight for democracy inside Hong Kong
gist: A profile of Hong Kong barrister and activist Chow Hang-tung, convicted of 'inciting subversion' on 21st August 2026 after five years in pre-trial detention, set against an accelerating national-security crackdown that has expanded the chief executive’s powers and dismantled most of the city’s democracy movement.

insights.claim: Hong Kong authorities recently expanded the national security law to let the region’s chief executive reclassify any criminal case as a matter of national security.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: A discretionary reclassification power raises legal and political risk for anyone operating in or with Hong Kong.
insights.locator: Chow’s verdict comes amid an accelerating crackdown

insights.claim: Chow Hang-tung was charged with 'inciting subversion' under the Beijing-imposed national security law in 2021, convicted on 21st August 2026, and now faces up to ten years in prison.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Marks how far the crackdown now reaches even individual, symbolic acts of dissent.

insights.claim: Organising the annual Victoria Park vigil commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre landed Chow and two fellow activists in detention.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Shows commemoration itself has been criminalised, signalling the shrinking space for civil society.
insights.locator: Later in life, organising this annual vigil

insights.claim: Chow was criticised by fellow Hong Kong activists for prioritising mainland Chinese dissidents’ rights, but activist Patrick Poon calls her 'prophetic' for seeing how the fate of mainland dissidents foreshadowed Hong Kong’s.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Frames mainland repression as a leading indicator for what spreads to previously autonomous jurisdictions.

insights.claim: Chow trained as a geophysicist and seismologist at Cambridge before retraining as a barrister in the mid-2010s, turning to human rights after judging the government worsened the 2008 Sichuan earthquake’s impact.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Context on the making of a durable, self-directed dissident who represents herself in court.
insights.locator: In 2007, Chow received a postgraduate scholarship

insights.claim: Chow chose to represent herself and used her final submission to argue that the case was in effect a trial of the national security law itself and to question whether the judiciary had become a tool of continued CCP rule.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Signals that Hong Kong’s courts are now themselves contested terrain in the legitimacy fight.
insights.quote: a trial on this law itself

insights.claim: Chow’s fiancé, Chinese dissident Ye Du, is barred from leaving China and under strict surveillance, and the couple have been unable to communicate since February of the prior year.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Illustrates the reach of cross-border repression against dissidents’ networks and families.
insights.locator: her fiancé Ye Du tells me

insights.claim: Despite her conviction, Chow refuses to lose hope, locating it in the resilience of ordinary people rather than in political prediction.
insights.speaker: Frankie Vetch
insights.so_what: Captures the enduring soft-power cost to Beijing of visible, unbroken defiance.
insights.quote: No one can predict the future, but we should not lose our confidence in the people, who are where hope lies
insights.locator: In the days before her conviction
